summary: Describes using AES counter mode, with an explicit initialization vector, as a confidentiality mechanism in IPsec's Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP). It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC shows how to use AES in counter mode to encrypt IPsec packets. In counter mode, AES encrypts a running number to produce a stream of random-looking bytes, and the payload is combined with that stream. The RFC also spells out the mistakes that break the scheme, chiefly reusing an initialization vector or a key, which lets anyone who sees two packets work out what was inside them.

subtitle: How to encrypt IPsec packets with AES in counter mode, and the traps that make it unsafe if misused.

tldr.problem: IPsec needs a way to encrypt a packet, and AES in counter mode is fast, but a counter mode cipher is easy to use in a way that destroys the protection it is supposed to give.
tldr.mechanism: AES-CTR turns AES into a stream cipher: each packet carries an 8-octet initialization vector, the counter block combines a 32-bit nonce, that vector and a 32-bit block counter, and the payload is XORed with the resulting key stream.
tldr.outcome: The RFC fixes the exact layout, the key sizes and the key derivation from IKE, and then states the rules that make it safe: a fresh key per key exchange, a unique initialization vector per packet, a fresh unpredictable nonce per security association, and an authentication function alongside the encryption.

today:
RFC 3686 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, so it remains the document that defines AES counter mode with an explicit initialization vector as an IPsec ESP confidentiality mechanism.

The design rationale in the memo explains why the specification uses an explicit IV field rather than the ESP sequence number, and lists what that buys: only the encryptor has to guarantee uniqueness, any technique that produces a unique value per packet is allowed, the choice of technique stays inside the encryptor's assurance boundary, and the decryptor is unaffected by it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The National Institute of Standards and Technology selected the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES), also known as Rijndael. AES is a block cipher, and it can be used in many different modes. This document describes the use of AES Counter Mode (AES-CTR), with an explicit initialization vector, as an IPsec Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) confidentiality mechanism.

The document does not give an overview of IPsec. Information about how the various components of IPsec work together to provide security services is available in RFC 2401 and RFC 2411.
sections.plainLanguage: IPsec has a part called ESP that carries the protected payload. This RFC says how to fill that part when the cipher is AES run in counter mode, which is the fastest way to use AES on a network link.

sections.title: AES Counter Mode
sections.content:
NIST has defined five modes of operation for AES and other approved block ciphers: ECB, CBC, CFB, OFB and CTR. Only AES Counter mode is discussed here. AES-CTR requires the encryptor to generate a unique per-packet value and to communicate it to the decryptor, and this specification calls that value an initialization vector (IV). The same IV and key combination must not be used more than once. The encryptor can generate the IV in any manner that ensures uniqueness; common approaches include incrementing a counter for each packet and linear feedback shift registers.

The specification also calls for the use of a nonce for additional protection against precomputation attacks. The nonce need not be secret, but it must be unpredictable before the IPsec security association that uses AES-CTR is established.

AES-CTR uses the AES block cipher to create a stream cipher. Data is encrypted and decrypted by XORing with the key stream produced by AES encrypting sequential counter block values. AES-CTR is easy to implement, can be pipelined and parallelised, and supports key stream precomputation, which matters on fast links. It uses only the AES encrypt operation, for both encryption and decryption, so implementations are smaller than those of many other AES modes.

When used correctly, AES-CTR provides a high level of confidentiality. It is also easy to use incorrectly. Being a stream cipher, any reuse of the per-packet value with the same nonce and key is catastrophic: an IV collision immediately leaks information about the plaintext in both packets. For that reason it is inappropriate to use this mode with static keys, and implementations must use fresh keys with AES-CTR. IKE can be used to establish fresh keys and can also provide the nonce value.

With AES-CTR it is trivial to take a valid ciphertext and forge other ciphertexts that are also valid to the decryptor, so it is equally catastrophic to use AES-CTR without a companion authentication function. Implementations must use AES-CTR together with an authentication function, such as HMAC-SHA-1-96.
sections.plainLanguage: Counter mode turns a cipher that works on fixed-size blocks into one that works on any length of data. The cipher encrypts a counter, and the result is combined with the data. Each packet needs its own starting point, and that starting point must never be reused with the same key, or two packets end up protected by the same random-looking stream, which is what makes the data readable again.

sections.title: Key Size, Rounds and Block Size
sections.content:
AES supports three key sizes: 128 bits, 192 bits and 256 bits. The default key size is 128 bits, and all implementations must support it; implementations may also support the 192-bit and 256-bit sizes.

AES uses a different number of rounds for each key size. With a 128-bit key, implementations must use 10 rounds. With a 192-bit key, they must use 12 rounds. With a 256-bit key, they must use 14 rounds.

The AES block size is 128 bits, or 16 octets, so each AES encrypt operation generates 128 bits of key stream. AES-CTR encryption is the XOR of the key stream with the plaintext, and decryption is the XOR of the key stream with the ciphertext. If the generated key stream is longer than the plaintext or the ciphertext, the extra bits are simply discarded. For that reason AES-CTR does not require the plaintext to be padded to a multiple of the block size, although padding may be included to provide limited traffic flow confidentiality, as specified in the ESP specification.
sections.plainLanguage: AES can use keys of three lengths, and the longer the key the more rounds the cipher runs, which is what makes the key harder to guess. The cipher always works on 16-byte blocks, and in counter mode those blocks are what the key stream is made of.

sections.title: The ESP Payload
sections.content:
The ESP payload is the initialization vector followed by the ciphertext. The initialization vector field must be eight octets. The IV must be chosen by the encryptor in a manner that ensures that the same IV value is used only once for a given key, and the encryptor can generate it in any manner that ensures uniqueness, such as incrementing a counter for each packet or using a linear feedback shift register. Including the IV in each packet ensures that the decryptor can generate the key stream needed for decryption, even when some packets are lost or reordered.

The encrypted payload contains the ciphertext. AES-CTR mode does not require plaintext padding, but ESP does require padding to 32-bit word-align the authentication data. The padding, the Pad Length and the Next Header must be concatenated with the plaintext before encryption, as described in the ESP specification.

Since it is trivial to construct a forgery from an AES-CTR ciphertext, AES-CTR implementations must employ a non-NULL ESP authentication method, and HMAC-SHA-1-96 is a likely choice.
sections.plainLanguage: Every protected packet carries the eight bytes that say where its key stream starts, then the encrypted data, then a check that proves the packet was not altered. The receiver uses the eight bytes to rebuild the same key stream and reverse the encryption, one packet at a time.

sections.title: The Counter Block Format
sections.content:
Each packet conveys the IV needed to construct the sequence of counter blocks that produce the key stream. The AES counter block is 128 bits, and it has three parts.

The Nonce field is 32 bits. The nonce is a single use value, so a fresh nonce must be assigned for each security association, at the beginning of that association. It need not be secret, but it must be unpredictable before the beginning of the security association.

The Initialization Vector field is 64 bits, and the same IV value must be used only once for a given key.

The Block Counter field is the least significant 32 bits of the counter block. It begins with the value one and is incremented to generate subsequent portions of the key stream, and it is a 32-bit big-endian integer.

This construction permits each packet to consist of up to (2^32)-1 blocks, which is 4,294,967,295 blocks or 68,719,476,720 octets. That is enough key stream for each packet to handle any IPv6 jumbogram.
sections.plainLanguage: The counter block is the number that gets encrypted to produce the key stream. It is built from three pieces: a nonce that is fresh for each security association, the per-packet initialization vector, and a counter that starts at one and goes up for each block of the payload.

sections.title: IKE Conventions
sections.content:
Implementations must use fresh keys with AES-CTR, and IKE can be used to establish them. The conventions for obtaining the unpredictable nonce value from IKE are given here, and they produce a nonce value that is secret as well as unpredictable.

IKE makes use of a pseudo-random function to derive keying material, called KEYMAT, and keying material is extracted from the output string without regard to boundaries. The size of the requested KEYMAT must be four octets longer than is needed for the associated AES key, and the keying material is used as follows. For AES-CTR with a 128-bit key, the KEYMAT requested for each key is 20 octets: the first 16 are the 128-bit AES key and the remaining four are the nonce value in the counter block. For a 192-bit key, 28 octets are requested, the first 24 being the key and the last four the nonce. For a 256-bit key, 36 octets are requested, the first 32 being the key and the last four the nonce.

The document does not specify conventions for using AES-CTR in IKE Phase 1 negotiations, and says a separate specification is needed, along with an Encryption Algorithm Identifier. For IKE Phase 2 negotiations, IANA has assigned an ESP Transform Identifier of 13 for AES-CTR with an explicit IV. Since AES supports three key lengths, the Key Length attribute must be specified in the IKE Phase 2 exchange, and its value must be 128, 192 or 256.
sections.plainLanguage: The keys and the nonce come from the key exchange, not from the packet format. IKE is told to produce a little more keying material than the cipher key needs, and the extra four bytes are the nonce. The document also names the code number that identifies this cipher when two nodes negotiate.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
When used properly, AES-CTR mode provides strong confidentiality, and work by Bellare, Desai, Jokipii and Rogaway shows that the privacy guarantees of counter mode are at least as strong as those of CBC mode with the same block cipher. It is also very easy to misuse it. If counter block values are used for more than one packet with the same key, the same key stream is used to encrypt both packets and the confidentiality guarantees are voided.

The document shows the arithmetic. If two plaintexts are encrypted with the same key stream, then XORing the two ciphertexts together cancels the key stream and leaves the two plaintexts XORed together, and once an attacker has that, separating the plaintexts is relatively straightforward. Using any stream cipher, including AES-CTR, to encrypt two plaintexts under the same key stream leaks the plaintext. Stream ciphers, including AES-CTR, should therefore not be used with static keys, and ESP implementations must use fresh keys with AES-CTR, which IKE can establish. IKE can also establish the nonce at the beginning of the security association. Where a mechanism other than IKE establishes a single key for both directions, there is a high probability that the peers select the same IV values for some packets, so implementations that use the same key for outbound and inbound traffic with the same peer must ensure that the two peers assign different nonce values.

Data forgery is trivial with CTR mode, for the same reason, so ESP implementations must use AES-CTR in conjunction with ESP authentication. In addition, because AES has a 128-bit block size, the ciphertext becomes distinguishable from random values after 2^64 blocks are encrypted with a single key, and since ESP with Extended Sequence Numbers allows up to 2^64 packets in a single security association, there is real potential for more than 2^64 blocks to be encrypted with one key. Implementations should generate a fresh key before 2^64 blocks are encrypted with the same key. ESP with 32-bit Sequence Numbers will not exceed 2^64 blocks even if all of the packets are maximum-length IPv6 jumbograms.

There are also generic precomputation attacks against all block cipher modes that allow a meet-in-the-middle attack against the key. Assuming the resources are available, the theoretical strength of AES-CTR, and of any other block cipher mode, is limited to 2^(n/2) bits, where n is the number of bits in the key. Long keys are the best countermeasure, and the unpredictable nonce value in the counter block significantly increases the size of the table an attacker must build.
sections.plainLanguage: Reusing a key stream is fatal, and the document works out why with the arithmetic: combining two ciphertexts that were protected by the same stream cancels the stream out and leaves the two plaintexts combined, which can then be taken apart. So each security association needs its own key, each packet its own starting value, and the encryption always needs an integrity check beside it.

sections.title: Design Rationale
sections.content:
The document explains why an explicit IV field is used rather than the ESP sequence number field, and lists the reasons. The choice is not a cryptographic security issue, since either approach prevents counter block collisions.

Only the encryptor can ensure that a value is not used for more than one packet, so there is no advantage to a mechanism that lets the decryptor detect collisions; the damage is done either way. The explicit IV allows any technique that meets the encryptor's time budget and produces a unique value per packet, such as adders, which are simple but do not run in constant time, or linear feedback shift registers, which do. The complexity stays with the implementer of the encryptor and does not make the decryptor's job harder. When the encryptor has more than one cryptographic hardware device, an IV prefix can be assigned to each device so that collisions cannot occur, and the decryptor does not need to examine the IV structure at all, which is not possible with sequence numbers because their semantics require sequential generation. Assurance boundaries matter too: the assignment of the per-packet counter block value needs to be inside the assurance boundary, and a sequence number collision does not have the dire consequences that a counter block collision has. Coupling the sequence number with the IV is possible where the sequence number is assigned inside the assurance boundary, and decoupling it is possible where it is not.

The overhead of 64 bits for the IV field is acceptable, and is significantly less than the overhead of Cipher Block Chaining mode, which normally requires a full block for the IV and, on average, half a block for padding. AES-CTR with an explicit IV has about one-third of the overhead of AES-CBC, and the overhead is constant for each packet. The inclusion of the nonce provides a weak countermeasure against precomputation attacks, and long keys provide a strong one. A 28-bit block counter value would be enough to encrypt the largest possible IPv6 jumbogram, but a 32-bit field is used because it is convenient for both hardware and software implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: Using the sequence number instead of a separate field would save eight bytes per packet, but it would tie the two together and force one particular way of generating the value. The document lists why the extra eight bytes are worth paying: the encryptor stays in charge, the choice of generator is left open, and the counter block value stays inside the part of the system that is formally evaluated.

data.title: Encryption of n plaintext blocks
data.code:
CTRBLK := NONCE || IV || ONE
FOR i := 1 to n-1 DO
  CT[i] := PT[i] XOR AES(CTRBLK)
  CTRBLK := CTRBLK + 1
END
CT[n] := PT[n] XOR TRUNC(AES(CTRBLK))

fields.name: Nonce
fields.desc: A single use value, fresh for each security association and unpredictable before it begins.

fields.name: Initialization Vector
fields.desc: The per-packet value, which must be used only once for a given key.

fields.name: Block Counter
fields.desc: A 32-bit big-endian integer that starts at one and is incremented for each block.

viz.caption: THE RULES THAT MAKE AES-CTR SAFE (RFC 3686)

items.title: Fresh keys
items.text: Implementations must use fresh keys with AES-CTR. Static keys are inappropriate, because reuse across power cycles cannot be prevented.

items.title: Unique IV per packet
items.text: The same IV value must be used only once for a given key, and it travels in the packet so the receiver can rebuild the key stream.

items.title: Fresh unpredictable nonce
items.text: A fresh nonce is assigned at the start of each security association and must be unpredictable before the association begins.

items.title: Authentication is required
items.text: AES-CTR must be used with a non-NULL ESP authentication method, because forging ciphertexts is otherwise trivial.

items.title: Fresh key before 2^64 blocks
items.text: A fresh key should be generated before 2^64 blocks are encrypted with the same key, since the ciphertext becomes distinguishable from random after that.
